catalog_quote: Ñ. has a terraced-level tone system with high and low tone, downstep, and downdrift. As is common with languages in the area, it employs a system of “advanced tongue root (ATR)” harmony restricting the co-occurrence of specific vowels within the same word. Vowels are: i, e, o, u [+ATR], ɪ, ɛ, a, ɔ, ʊ [-ATR]. Vowel length is distinctive in Ñ., as in ǧík ‘completely’ vs. ǧíík ‘always’. Before a pause, short vowels carrying a single (as opposed a complex) tone are devoiced: é-tál(ì) [étál̥ị̥] ‘custom’; such voiceless word-final vowels (here written between parentheses) are realized as extra-short voiced vowels before another word. [...] Case is marked by way of tonal inflection on noun phrases and pronouns

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nyangatom is described as a two-level (H/L) terraced tone language with downstep and downdrift, tone carrying grammatical load (case on nouns and pronouns, number marking per Moges 2023). No source examined says anything about word stress or accent; there is no statement that stress exists, where it falls, or that it is absent. Moges 2017 treats closed and long-vowel syllables as heavy (moraic weight) but does not connect weight to any prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the sources say nothing about stress. Moges 2023 (p. 44) adds that 'the analysis of tone in Nyangatom is at its early stage'.
new_statements.domain_note: Sketch statements are at word level (nouns, pronouns; tonal case inflection 'on noun phrases and pronouns'); devoicing rule is pre-pausal (phrase-final). Dimmendaal's data are the Ethiopian (Lower Omo) variety; Moges' data are from Ethiopian speakers, ca. 300 basic lexical items.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Nyangatom (Ñaŋatom, 'Bume') variety of the Lower Omo valley, SW Ethiopia; Dimmendaal 2007 also covers the neighbouring Sudan (South Sudan) speakers. Nyangatom belongs to the Teso-Turkana dialect cluster; Blench (2012, per Wikipedia) counts it as a dialect of Turkana (turk1308), and Moges 2016/2017 transfer Dimmendaal's (1983) Turkana phonological analyses to it. No sub-dialect is named in any source. Glottolog 5.1's two 'descriptive' refs are misleading: Tornay 1981 is an ethnographic outline (computer-assigned 'grammar sketch'), so the real descriptive corpus is Dimmendaal 2007, Schröder & Kadanya 2011 (unlocated) and Moges Yigezu's three SEL articles (2016, 2017, 2023).

sources.note: Two-page encyclopedia sketch; phonology paragraph: consonant inventory, 'terraced-level tone system with high and low tone, downstep, and downdrift', ATR harmony, distinctive vowel length, pre-pausal devoicing of short vowels carrying a single tone; case marked by tonal inflection. No mention of stress or accent. Source: archive.org item uhlig-siegbert-et-al.-eds.-encyclopaedia-aethiopica-vol.-3-he-n-2007 (folkscanomy user upload, publicly readable, no access restriction); only the two-page entry was kept (scanned text + 2 page images), the full scanned file was deleted.

Phonology section paraphrases Dimmendaal 2007 (10 vowels with ATR, contrastive length, pre-pausal devoicing of short vowels 'carrying a single, simple tone') and Moges 2016 (implosives); no statement on stress. Gave the open URL of Moges 2016.

sources.note: §8 'Tonal Modification' (p. 44): 'The analysis of tone in Nyangatom is at its early stage.. According to a brief grammatical sketch given by Dimmendaal (2007) Nyangatom has two tone levels, high and low as well as down step and down drift. As in many Nilotic languages, tone has a grammatical function.. case.. marked by way of tonal inflection'. Second-hand on tone; nothing on stress.
